home.heading: Already using ChatGPT? Point it at your company.
home.body: Aexy speaks MCP, so the assistant you already pay for can work inside your workspace — moving tickets, updating deals, reading sprints, drafting from real context — instead of you copying it into a chat window and pasting the answer back.

anyClient.title: The assistant you already have
anyClient.body: ChatGPT connects over HTTP. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and Codex run the server locally. Nothing new to learn.

realWork.title: It does the work, not just the reading
realWork.body: Move a task to In Review and assign it. Create a deal. Log a ticket. Query analytics. Not a chatbot bolted onto a search box.

oauth.title: Sign in, don't paste a key
oauth.body: ChatGPT registers itself and sends you to a consent screen where you pick one workspace. No API key to mint, store, or forget about.

revoke.title: You can take it back
revoke.body: Every connector is listed with the workspace it reaches and when it last ran. Revoking cuts it off immediately — it cannot quietly reconnect.

shot.heading: The tool catalogue your assistant sees.
shot.body: Aexy ships an MCP server covering sprints, CRM, agents, email, analytics, and workflows — grouped by category, with a copy-paste setup block per client.

faq.question: Can I use Aexy from ChatGPT or Claude?
faq.answer: Yes. Aexy ships an MCP server, so ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Codex can work inside your workspace directly — reading sprints, moving tickets, updating CRM records, querying analytics. ChatGPT connects over a remote HTTP endpoint with OAuth: it registers itself, you approve one workspace on a consent screen, and the access it gets is scoped to you in that workspace and revocable at any time under Settings → Connected Apps.

prompts.heading: Things you can just ask for
prompts.body: Each of these lands on a real tool call against your workspace, under your own permissions.
prompts.sprint: Move the auth-refresh bug to In Review and assign it to Priya.
prompts.standup: What shipped in this sprint, and what is still open?
prompts.crm: Log a call with Northwind and set the deal to Negotiation.
prompts.ticket: Open a ticket for the login timeout and tag it urgent.
prompts.docs: Find our incident runbook and summarise the escalation path.
prompts.analytics: Who is over capacity this sprint?

capabilities.heading: What makes it safe to connect

anyClient.title: Any MCP client
anyClient.body: ChatGPT over remote HTTP; Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and Codex over a local process. One server, six ways in.

scoped.title: Scoped to one workspace
scoped.body: You pick the workspace at the consent screen. The grant is bound to you in that workspace — not to your account across everything you can reach.

filtered.title: Filtered before it is offered
filtered.body: Capabilities resolve from the same app access that governs the web app. Holding the sprints app is what grants sprint tools. What you cannot use is never offered.

audit.title: Listed, and revocable
audit.body: Connected Apps shows every client you authorised and when it last ran. Revoking kills the refresh token too, so it has to ask again.

connect.heading: Two ways to connect
connect.body: Which one you get depends on your client, and the difference matters.

remote.title: ChatGPT — remote, over OAuth
remote.body: Paste the server URL into Settings → Connectors → Create. ChatGPT registers itself, you approve one workspace, and the access is scoped to you there and revocable from Connected Apps. There is no API key in this flow.

local.title: Claude, Cursor, Codex — local process
local.body: These launch the server on your machine with an API token. Convenient for editors, but the token carries everything your account can do — treat it like a password and revoke it when the machine goes away.

security.heading: Governance, not a trust exercise
security.body: An MCP grant is the app grant your workspace already made. There is no second permission model to configure, drift from, or forget to revoke when somebody changes teams.

points.one: Authorization is OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, and every code and token is stored only as a digest.
points.two: Replaying an authorization code or a retired refresh token revokes the whole grant, because a replayed secret means somebody else is holding it.
points.three: Revoked connectors stay listed rather than disappearing, so an audit can see what existed and when it last ran.

q1.q: Do I need to install anything for ChatGPT?
q1.a: No. ChatGPT reaches Aexy over HTTP — you paste a URL into Settings → Connectors and approve a workspace. The local install applies only to editor clients like Claude Code, Cursor and Codex.

q2.q: Can a connector see data I cannot?
q2.a: No. Tools are built from the capabilities you already hold in the workspace you approved, and filtered before the client ever sees the list. A client that ignores the list gains nothing — every endpoint still enforces its own permissions.

q3.a: Settings → Connected Apps lists every client you authorised. Revoking invalidates both the access token and the refresh token behind it, so the client cannot mint a replacement — it has to walk the consent flow again.

q4.q: Does this work with self-hosted Aexy?
q4.a: Yes. The MCP server and its authorization endpoints are part of Aexy itself, so a self-hosted deployment exposes them at its own domain. Aexy is open source and self-hostable.

finalCta.heading: Connect it in about a minute.
finalCta.body: Start free, open Settings → Connected Apps, and point your assistant at your workspace.
